newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Single page of each U.N. document said to be $916.
newsitem.headline: Single page of each U.N. document said to be $916.

text.p: It costs $916 to produce each page of the mountain of U.N. documents issued in the organisation's six official languages, and each meeting costs $4,553, according to the chairman of the U.N. Committee on Conferences.

In a recent letter urging cost-saving measures, El Hassane Zahid, a member of Morocco's delegation, said many U.N. bodies seemed to be under the impression that conference-servicing resources were abundant, if not unlimited.
"In fact, the demand for services continues to grow even as the organisation endeavours to cut back in response to the increasingly severe financial constraints it is experiencing," he wrote.

As an example, he said the "notional cost of a single page of documentation in the six official languages is $916, of which $602 stems from translation." The rest is accounted for by such things as editing, reproduction and distribution.
The official U.N. languages are Arabic, Chinese, English, French, Russian and Spanish.
Zahid also said the "notional cost of one meeting is $4,553, of which $4,194 stems from interpretation."
Speeches in one of the official languages are normally interpreted simultaneously into the other five, enabling delegates to follow using earphones.
A U.N. official said more than 5,000 meetings serviced by U.N. staff were held at headquarters in New York each year.

Zahid said the 21-member Committee on Conferences, which acts as a sort of traffic monitor coordinating the scheduling of meetings, several years ago suggested the U.N. should make use of at least 80 percent of its allocated conference resources.

But in 1995 the rate of utilization at U.N. headquarters in New York and at U.N. centres in Geneva and Vienna was down to 76 percent, "owing to late starting and early ending of meetings and sessions and repeated cancellation of meetings."

"Here is another eye-opening figure," he continued. "If the start of every meeting in New York during a calendar year were delayed 10 minutes, the loss in unutilized conference-servicing resources would amount to around $875,000."
Listing what he called "common-sense solutions to conserve resources," he said U.N. bodies could review their needs with the aim of making better use of services.
"As for tactics to save time, experience shows that the chairman's presence in the conference room sets an example for other delegates to arrive punctually," he said.

Full use of meeting room time could be ensured if meetings were convened only when an adequate number of speakers were inscribed on the list and if several items were placed on the agenda. Sessions could possibly be shortened if a time limit for speakers were set, he added.

"The key to the success of this operation to consolidate limited resources is the will to redouble efforts so as to reverse a critical situation," he added in a one-and-a-half page document which, according to his calculations, cost close to $1,400 to produce.
